target_identification.speaker: Jane
target_identification.anchor_quote:
There is no dishonour, no breach of promise, no desertion in the case.
I am not under the slightest obligation to go to India, especially with
strangers. With you I would have ventured much, because I admire,
confide in, and, as a sister, I love you; but I am convinced that, go
when and with whom I would, I should not live long in that climate.

T.reason: This is an explicit avowal of Jane's loving emotional attitude toward St John. The qualification “as a sister” identifies the love as familial or sisterly rather than romantic, but does not weaken its truth-presenting force.

evidence.quotation:
because I admire,

P.reason: The focal expression undertakes no obligation. Jane uses the avowal to explain why she would have trusted St John, while expressly denying any promise or duty to go to India. A separate earlier offer to assist him must not be transferred onto “I love you.”

evidence.quotation: as a sister, I love you

original_speech_situation: Jane is resisting St John's claim that she has promised missionary service and his insistence that she marry him. She avows sisterly love as part of explaining why she would have ventured with him personally, while denying that she is obligated to go to India, especially with strangers.
undertaking_and_uptake: The focal “I love you” makes no undertaking. Jane's wider discussion had included willingness to accompany St John only in a non-marital assisting role, which he rejected as unsuitable. In this focal turn she explicitly denies any promise or obligation and describes what she “would have ventured” with him; St John does not accept a commitment but instead challenges her fear and then condemns her attachment to Mr Rochester.
recognition_note: I recognise the supplied text as Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre. The classification relies only on the supplied passages.
limitations: The evidence strongly supports a sincere sisterly or friendly affection, but it does not make the avowal romantic; indeed, the supplied context repeatedly distinguishes Jane's sisterly regard from marital love. The focal expression alone does not establish any promise, future action, or reciprocal affection from St John.
